schools.name: Presocratics
schools.description: The first Greek thinkers to explain the natural world and its principles by reasoned inquiry rather than myth.
schools.debatable: A modern label, not a school: SEP notes the last 'Presocratics' were contemporaries of Socrates. The Sophists are folded in here (SEP covers them in the same entry, §9).
questions: Underneath all the change I see, what is everything really made of?
Can I explain a rainbow or a storm without saying the gods did it?
How far can my senses, and my own reasoning, get me to the truth?

questionSources.section: 3. Xenophanes of Colophon and Heraclitus of Ephesus
3. Xenophanes of Colophon and Heraclitus of Ephesus

themes.name: Nature without myth
themes.text: These thinkers saw the world as a kosmos: an ordered, natural arrangement that makes sense on its own terms. Where the old poets had gods stepping in, they looked for causes inside nature itself. Xenophanes, for example, said the rainbow is simply coloured cloud.

themes.name: What things are made of
themes.text: Many of them looked for one basic stuff or principle (the Greeks called it the archē) behind everything. Thales is reported to have said water; Heraclitus pointed to fire; the atomists said tiny solid bodies moving in empty space.

themes.name: Everything flows
themes.text: Heraclitus taught that the world is constant change held together by a hidden order, which he called the logos (the rational account of how things work). Opposites like up and down, or waking and sleeping, turn out to be bound together.

sources.section: 3. Xenophanes of Colophon and Heraclitus of Ephesus

themes.name: Reality versus appearance
themes.text: Parmenides argued that real knowledge is about what is and cannot fail to be, and that the senses give us only belief. Democritus also split appearance from reality: tastes and colours are a matter of convention, while what really exists is atoms and void.

themes.name: Caring for the soul
themes.text: Natural inquiry sat alongside questions about how to live. Pythagoras seems to have taught that the soul is reborn after death and founded a strict way of life; Heraclitus thought a dry, fiery soul was wisest; Democritus was linked with the ideal of good cheer.

sources.section: 3. Xenophanes of Colophon and Heraclitus of Ephesus

reactedAgainst.text: The god-filled stories of poets like Hesiod, where the world comes from divine family feuds and the gods meddle in the weather and in human life.

sources.section: 9. Diogenes of Apollonia and the Sophists

schools.name: Socrates and Plato
schools.dateRange: late 5th–4th century BCE (Plato's Academy continues after him)
schools.description: Socrates' questioning method and Plato's dialogues, with the theory of Forms at their centre.
schools.debatable: The owner's sample had one 'Classical Greek' node; it is split here into Socrates/Plato and Aristotle because later schools attach to them differently (Neoplatonism to Plato, Scholasticism to Aristotle). SEP gives Plato's birth as 429? (Plato entry) and 424/3 (Socrates entry).
questions: Is a life I never stop to examine really worth living?
Do I actually know the things I think I know?
Is there a truer reality behind the world I see and touch?

themes.name: Question everything
themes.text: Socrates tested people's beliefs by cross-examining them, a method called the elenchus (asking 'what is it?' and then probing the answer). He claimed no expert knowledge himself; his wisdom was knowing that he did not know.

sources.section: a. The Elenchus: Socrates the Refuter

themes.name: Care for your soul
themes.text: Socrates urged his fellow Athenians to care for their souls more than for money, reputation or their bodies. Plato went further and treated the soul as a different kind of thing from the body, able to exist without it.

sources.section: ii. Priority of the Care of the Soul

themes.name: Virtue is knowledge
themes.text: Socrates argued that the virtues are really one, and that virtue is a kind of knowledge. On this view no one does wrong knowingly; doing wrong is a failure to know what is good.

sources.section: i. Unity of Virtue; All Virtue is Knowledge
ii. No One Errs Knowingly/No One Errs Willingly

themes.name: The Forms
themes.text: Plato held that the world of the senses is flawed, and that behind it stand the Forms: eternal, unchanging patterns like beauty or justice itself. Beautiful things are beautiful because they relate to Beauty itself.

themes.name: Who was the real Socrates?
themes.text: Socrates wrote nothing, so we meet him through others, mainly Plato and Xenophon, whose portraits differ a lot. Untangling the historical man from these portraits is called the Socratic problem, and it may never be solved.

sources.section: 2. The Socratic problem: Who was Socrates really?

reactedAgainst.text: The Sophists, paid teachers who claimed to teach success and virtue, and the earlier thinkers' focus on the heavens rather than on how to live.

sources.section: a. Presocratic Philosophy and the Sophists
2. The Socratic problem: Who was Socrates really?

schools.name: Aristotle and the Peripatetics
schools.description: Aristotle's systematic philosophy of logic, nature, ethics and metaphysics, taught at his school, the Lyceum.
schools.debatable: Usually treated as one great thinker rather than a school; the Lyceum/Peripatetic school gives it school status.
questions: What does a human life need in order to go well?
When I ask why something is the way it is, what would count as a full answer?
Do living things grow toward goals, even if nobody designed them?

questionSources.section: 7. The Four Causal Account of Explanatory Adequacy

themes.name: Start from wonder
themes.text: Aristotle thought philosophy begins in wonder at puzzling things. He trusted our senses and minds to be mostly reliable, so he started from how the world appears and what others had said about it, then worked through the puzzles.

themes.name: Four kinds of 'why'
themes.text: To explain a thing fully, Aristotle asked four questions: what it is made of, what form or pattern it has, what brought it about, and what it is for. A bronze statue, for example, has bronze, a shape, a sculptor and a purpose.

sources.section: 7. The Four Causal Account of Explanatory Adequacy

themes.name: Purpose in nature
themes.text: Aristotle held that nature works toward ends without any designer: leaves grow to shade fruit, spiders spin webs for a reason. His successor Theophrastus asked whether every natural thing really has a purpose.

themes.name: Flourishing in a community
themes.text: The best life is eudaimonia (happiness or flourishing): using reason, and using it excellently, over a whole life. Humans are political animals who flourish only inside a well-ordered city.

themes.name: The soul as the body's form
themes.text: For Aristotle the soul is not a separate thing living in the body but the form that makes a body alive and organized. Alexander of Aphrodisias later read the human soul as the perishable form of the body.

reactedAgainst.text: Plato's separate Forms, which Aristotle thought could not explain change, and the earlier thinkers who explained life by matter alone.

schools.name: Epicureanism
schools.dateRange: late 4th century BCE – Roman era (Lucretius, Philodemus 1st c. BCE)
schools.description: Atomist materialism joined to an ethics of tranquil pleasure and freedom from fear of death and the gods.
questions: Why should I not be afraid of death?
Which pleasures actually make a life happy, and which just leave me wanting more?
If the gods don't run the world, how should I think about them?

themes.name: Atoms and the void
themes.text: Everything, the soul included, is made of tiny indivisible particles (atoms) moving through empty space. Epicurus took this picture from earlier atomists like Democritus and reworked it. Knowing how nature works is meant to free us from fear.

themes.name: Death is nothing to us
themes.text: Because the soul is made of atoms that scatter when we die, there is no afterlife and no punishment waiting. While we exist, death is not here; when death comes, we are not. Lucretius adds that we don't mind the time before we were born, so why mind the time after?

themes.name: Pleasure as calm
themes.text: The goal is happiness, understood as freedom from bodily pain and mental disturbance (ataraxia, peace of mind). This is not a life of chasing thrills: empty desires like fame or great wealth can never be satisfied, so wisdom means telling desires apart.

themes.name: Friendship and community
themes.text: Epicurus valued friendship extremely highly and encouraged followers to live in communities. Philodemus wrote on how such a community should work, including the skill of frank, caring criticism among friends.

themes.name: Gods without fear
themes.text: Epicureans did believe in gods, but gods who live in perfect peace and take no part in running the world, neither rewarding nor punishing. Fear of angry, meddling gods is a false belief that makes people miserable.

reactedAgainst.text: Plato's Forms and the belief in an immortal soul facing punishment after death, which Epicurus saw as the deep root of human anxiety.

sources.section: 3.417–829: Thirty proofs of the mortality of soul

schools.name: Stoicism
schools.description: A unified system of logic, physics and ethics teaching that virtue, living in agreement with a rational nature, is the only good.
questions: What in my life is actually up to me?
Can I still be happy if I lose my health, money or good name?
If everything is fated, am I still responsible for what I do?

themes.name: Living in agreement with nature
themes.text: Zeno called the goal of life 'living in agreement': one consistent reason, never at war with itself. Later Stoics added 'with nature', meaning bringing your own reason in tune with the reason that runs the whole cosmos.

themes.name: Virtue is the only good
themes.text: Health, wealth and reputation are 'indifferents': worth choosing in normal life, but they never make you happier or unhappier. Only virtue, the perfected state of reason, is truly good, so happiness is in your own power.

themes.name: Emotions are judgments
themes.text: For the Stoics, passions like fear or anger are not forces that ambush us; they follow from judgments we assent to, usually false ones about what is good or bad. Change the judgment and the emotion changes. The wise person has calm 'good feelings' instead.

themes.name: Fate and what is up to us
themes.text: Everything happens through an unbreakable chain of causes, which the Stoics call fate. Yet whether we assent to an impression (how something appears to us) is up to us, and that is where responsibility lives.

themes.name: Citizens of the world
themes.text: Because all humans share reason, they are fellow citizens, together with Zeus, of one world-city (a cosmopolis). Justice therefore reaches every human being, not just your own city.

sources.section: 3. Justice: Acting for the Sake of the Cosmopolis

reactedAgainst.text: The Peripatetic and Academic view that 'external goods' like health and wealth add to happiness; the Stoics also competed with Epicurus's school, founded in Athens just before theirs.

sources.section: 5.3 On Renaissance and Early Modern Philosophy

schools.name: Ancient Skepticism
schools.description: Academic and Pyrrhonian skeptics who suspended judgment, arguing that no claim to knowledge is secure.
schools.debatable: Two movements (Academic and Pyrrhonian) under one node; SEP treats them in one entry.
questions: Can I ever be sure that the way something looks to me is true?
Can I live and act without firm beliefs?
Could giving up the hunt for certainty bring me peace of mind?

themes.name: Suspending judgment
themes.text: The skeptics' key move is epochē (suspension of judgment): neither affirming nor denying a claim once you have weighed it. 'Skeptic' originally just meant inquirer, someone who keeps investigating.

sources.section: 3.2 What is the Skeptical ability or skill?

themes.name: No sure test of truth
themes.text: The Stoics claimed some impressions are so clear they cannot be false. The Academic skeptics replied that a false impression could always look just the same, so there is no reliable test of truth (a 'criterion').

themes.name: Arguing both sides
themes.text: Skeptics trained themselves to set an equally strong argument against every argument. Carneades is said to have argued for justice one day in Rome and against it the next.

sources.section: 3.2 What is the Skeptical ability or skill?

themes.name: Peace of mind
themes.text: Pyrrhonian skeptics aimed at tranquility (ataraxia). Troubled by conflicting appearances, they hoped to settle what is true, found the arguments balanced, suspended judgment, and found calm followed.

themes.name: Living by appearances
themes.text: Critics said a person without beliefs could not act. Skeptics answered that you can be guided by what appears to you, or by what is persuasive, without claiming it is true.

reactedAgainst.text: The 'dogmatists', especially the Stoics, who claimed that certain impressions give a sure test of truth; Arcesilaus thought Zeno far too confident about our powers of knowing.

sources.section: 4.2 Aenesidemus, the Ten Modes, and Appearances
5.1 Augustine: Re-Conceiving Skepticism in a Theological Framework

schools.name: Neoplatonism
schools.description: A late-antique Platonism deriving all reality from a single first principle, the One.
schools.debatable: The name is modern; its members called themselves simply Platonists (SEP).
questions: How could a whole, varied universe come from one single source?
If everything flows from the Good, where does evil come from?
If I am more than my body, what is my life really for?

themes.name: The One beyond being
themes.text: Everything depends on a single first principle, called the One or the Good. It is so simple and so far beyond ordinary things that almost nothing can be said about it, except that it is absolute unity.

themes.name: Unfolding in stages
themes.text: Reality pours out of the One in steps, not all at once: first Intellect (pure consciousness), then Soul, then the living world. Each level then turns back toward its source, a pattern they called procession and return.

themes.name: Mind before matter
themes.text: They held that consciousness comes first and the physical world is its outer effect. Matter is the faint edge where this outflow runs out, like darkness at the end of light.

themes.name: Climbing back to the divine
themes.text: The goal of life is to return the divine in us to its source. Plotinus and Porphyry trusted philosophy for this climb, while Iamblichus and Proclus gave priority to theurgy (ritual acts done together with the gods).

themes.name: Harmonising the whole tradition
themes.text: These Platonists tried to weave nearly all earlier Greek thought, myth and religion into one system. Porphyry argued that Plato and Aristotle agree on essentials, and Proclus sought harmony between old religious revelations and Plato.

sources.section: 3.4.3 The Harmony of Plato and Aristotle

reactedAgainst.text: It rejected the materialism of the Epicureans and the Stoics' view that everything real is a body, and Plotinus strongly opposed Gnosticism (a movement that saw the world as a flawed creation).

schools.name: Early Christian Philosophy (Patristic)
schools.description: The Church Fathers and their heirs, who used Greek philosophy, above all Platonism, to think through Christian faith.
schools.debatable: A period and a group of Christian authors rather than a school; SEP has no 'Patristic' entry, so it rests on the Augustine, Origen, Boethius, Pseudo-Dionysius and Medieval Philosophy entries. Boethius and Augustine are often counted as the start of medieval philosophy.
questions: If God is good and made everything, where does evil come from?
If God already knows what I will do, am I still free?
Should I believe first and understand later, or the other way round?

themes.name: Greek philosophy serving faith
themes.text: These Christian thinkers used Greek philosophy, above all Platonism, as a tool for explaining scripture and doctrine. Philosophy was a respected helper, but scripture had the final word.

themes.name: Faith seeking understanding
themes.text: Belief comes first in time, but understanding is the goal. Reason is a gift to be used to grasp what one already accepts in faith, not a rival to it.

themes.name: Evil as missing goodness
themes.text: Evil is not a thing or substance in its own right. It is a lack or corruption of goodness, which keeps God from being its author.

themes.name: Speaking of a God beyond words
themes.text: God is greater than any name we can give. One can praise God with names, but in the end every name, and even every denial, has to be left behind.

themes.name: Foreknowledge and freedom
themes.text: If God knows everything in advance, can people still choose? Boethius answered that God sees all of time at once, as one eternal present, so his knowing does not force our choices.

reactedAgainst.text: It pushed back against dualist and Gnostic views that blamed evil on a rival power or a split within God, and against skeptics who said truth cannot be known.

sources.section: 2.2 The Rule and Two Exceptions: Latin Philosophy, 800–1100

schools.name: Scholasticism
schools.dateRange: c. 1100–1500 (within a medieval period of roughly 500–1500)
schools.description: University philosophy of the Latin Middle Ages, reconciling Aristotle's newly recovered works with Christian theology by commentary and disputation.
schools.debatable: A method and institution (the schools and universities) more than a doctrine; SEP's entry is 'Medieval Philosophy', of which scholasticism is the Latin university strand. Augustine and Boethius belong to the earlier medieval period.
questions: Can reason prove that God exists, or must I take it on faith?
When I call two cats 'cats', is there a real catness they share, or just a word?
If a pagan philosopher's argument seems sound, can it clash with what faith teaches?

themes.name: Aristotle in the university
themes.text: As Aristotle's full works reached Latin Europe, the new universities built their arts teaching around him. Thinkers worked out how this pagan philosopher fitted with Christian teaching.

themes.name: Reasoning through authorities
themes.text: Much philosophy was done as commentary on respected texts, which often led to new ideas. Abelard's method of reconciling texts that seem to contradict each other, by careful analysis of concepts, became the basis of later theology.

themes.name: Faith seeking understanding
themes.text: Faith was the starting point, and reason was used to understand it more deeply. Several thinkers offered proofs that God exists, from Anselm's argument from the idea of God to Aquinas' arguments from a first cause.

sources.section: 2.1 “Faith Seeking Understanding”: The character and purpose of Anselm’s theistic proofs

themes.name: The problem of universals
themes.text: Is there something real, like humanity, shared by Socrates and Plato, or only a shared word or concept? Scotus said yes, there is a real common nature; Abelard and Ockham said no.

themes.name: Will, freedom and God's choices
themes.text: Later thinkers stressed God's free will and power. Scotus made God's will the ground of good and evil and saw human freedom as having real options at the very moment of choice; Ockham followed him on God's will.

reactedAgainst.text: It answered both those who wanted no reasoning in matters of faith and those who followed Aristotle even where he contradicted Christian teaching, aiming instead to make reason and faith agree.

sources.section: 1.2 The Platonic Schools of Late Antiquity

schools.name: Renaissance Philosophy
schools.description: A return to classical Greek and Roman sources and to ethics and eloquence, set against scholastic logic and university learning.
schools.debatable: IEP's 'Renaissance Philosophy' has humanism as one current beside Renaissance Aristotelianism, Platonism (Ficino) and revived Hellenistic schools; the node covers them all.
questions: What good is philosophy if it doesn't help me live a better life?
Should I trust the textbooks, or go back and read the original sources myself?
Given how limited we are, can we know anything for certain at all?

themes.name: Back to the sources
themes.text: Thinkers prized ancient Greek and Roman texts and read them in the original languages. Close study of language became a tool for criticism, as when Valla exposed a forged document and Erasmus edited the Greek New Testament.

themes.name: Philosophy for living well
themes.text: Humanists cared most about moral philosophy and wrote for a general audience. Their aim was to make people and cities more virtuous, not to solve technical puzzles.

themes.name: Persuasion over formal logic
themes.text: Humanists mocked the logic taught in universities. Valla and others wanted arguments judged by how well they persuade and work in real debate, with logic serving rhetoric.

themes.name: Plato reborn
themes.text: Platonism returned as a rival to Aristotle. Ficino translated Plato and Plotinus, and Platonists read the dialogues as sacred mysteries pointing toward union with God.

themes.name: Old schools, new life
themes.text: Stoicism, Epicureanism and Skepticism were revived. Petrarch drew on Stoic remedies for distress, Valla built a Christian ethics of pleasure, and skeptical arguments were used in religious debates.

reactedAgainst.text: It reacted against scholastic Aristotelian philosophy, its technical logic and the university education built on it, which humanists saw as useless for living well.

schools.name: Rationalism
schools.description: The view that reason, independent of sense experience, is a key source of knowledge and concepts, some of them innate.
schools.debatable: 'Continental Rationalists' is a later historians' grouping (SEP), not a self-named school.
questions: Is there anything I can know with no room at all for doubt?
Are some ideas already in my mind before experience teaches me anything?
Does everything that happens have a reason why it is so and not otherwise?

themes.name: Reason over the senses
themes.text: Some knowledge comes from reason alone, not from the senses, and it is better than sense knowledge. For Descartes, what reason grasps is certain while the senses always leave some doubt.

themes.name: Ideas we are born with
themes.text: Some concepts or truths are part of our rational nature from the start, and experience only triggers our awareness of them. Descartes counted the idea of God as innate; Leibniz compared the mind to marble whose veins shape the statue.

themes.name: Intuition and deduction
themes.text: Knowledge is built like geometry: from truths seen directly by the mind (intuition), more truths are drawn out step by step (deduction). Rationalists claimed this works even for truths about God and the world.

themes.name: Systems from first principles
themes.text: Big systems were built from a few basic principles. Spinoza derived his Ethics from definitions and axioms like a geometry book, and Leibniz rested his on principles such as sufficient reason.

themes.name: Mind and body
themes.text: How do thinking and the physical world fit together? Descartes made them two separate substances, Spinoza two sides of one Nature, and Leibniz a harmony set up in advance by God.

reactedAgainst.text: It reacted against the scholastic Aristotelian view that all knowledge comes through the senses, which Descartes called a childhood prejudice.

schools.name: Empiricism
schools.description: The view that all our concepts and knowledge come ultimately from experience, not innate ideas.
schools.debatable: 'British Empiricists' is likewise a later historians' grouping (SEP).
questions: If I wasn't born with ideas, where does everything in my mind come from?
Why do I expect the future to be like the past?
Does a tree still exist when no one is perceiving it?

themes.name: The blank slate
themes.text: The mind starts empty and experience writes on it. Locke said all our basic ideas come from sensation (the senses) and reflection (noticing our own mental acts).

themes.name: No innate ideas
themes.text: Empiricists denied that any knowledge or concepts are inborn. Locke argued that if they were, children would know them, and they don't.

themes.name: Ideas are copies
themes.text: Hume held that every simple idea is a fainter copy of an earlier impression (a vivid feeling or perception). So experience also sets the limits of what our ideas can mean.

themes.name: Knowing the limits
themes.text: Before reaching for answers, we should check what our minds can handle. Some things we may never know, and belief should match the evidence.

themes.name: Cause and habit
themes.text: We never see a necessary link between cause and effect, only one thing regularly following another. Hume concluded that our idea of causation comes from a habit of expectation.

reactedAgainst.text: It reacted against the rationalist claim that some knowledge and ideas are innate, part of the mind before any experience.

schools.name: The Enlightenment and Kant
schools.dateRange: 18th century (roots in the 16th–17th-century scientific revolution; Kant's Critique 1781; ends roughly with the 1790s)
schools.description: A movement of confidence in reason and science to question traditional authority, ending in Kant's critical philosophy, which tested what reason itself can know.
schools.debatable: A period and movement, not a school; it spans rationalists, empiricists and skeptics. Kant is merged in here (decision L17); SEP's Kant entry places his Critique at the Enlightenment's end (§2.1), while IEP counts him as the first German Idealist.
questions: Why should I let a church, a king or tradition tell me what to believe, if I can work it out for myself?
If science explains nature with fixed laws, where do my freedom and my morals fit in?
How far can human reason really reach, and where does it run out?

questionSources.section: 1.4 Science of Man and Subjectivism in the Enlightenment

themes.name: Think for yourself
themes.text: Kant described enlightenment as growing out of a self-imposed immaturity: being unable to use your own understanding without someone else steering. Across the movement this meant trusting your own reason and experience over tradition, myth and prejudice.

themes.name: Science as the model
themes.text: The success of the new science, above all Newton's, made people confident that reason could understand nature and improve human life. Philosophy stopped being theology's servant and became an independent force that could challenge the old and build the new.

themes.name: Questioning church and crown
themes.text: Enlightenment thinkers found that political and religious authority often rested on myth and obscure tradition. Most attacked superstition, fanaticism and church power rather than religion as such, and many hoped for a purified, 'rational' religion.

themes.name: Gathering all knowledge
themes.text: The Encyclopedia, edited by Diderot and d'Alembert and published from 1751 to 1772, tried to collect human knowledge and pass it on to improve society. It was secular and quietly anti-authoritarian, so the French state censored it.

sources.section: 1.2 Ascendance as Writer and Philosophe through the Encyclopédie (1750–1765)

themes.name: Rights, consent and the social contract
themes.text: The period shaped the idea of government by consent of the governed, the ideals of freedom and equality, basic individual rights and religious toleration. Rousseau offered a contrasting model built on the general will, the will of citizens aimed at their common good.

sources.section: 3.1 The idea of the general will

reactedAgainst.text: The authority of tradition, the established church and absolute monarchy, and the superstition, prejudice and myth that were seen as competing with each person's own reason and experience.

sources.section: 1.4 Science of Man and Subjectivism in the Enlightenment
b. Dogmatic Slumber, Synthetic A Priori Knowledge, and the Copernican Shift

schools.name: German Idealism
schools.description: Fichte, Schelling and Hegel radicalised Kant into absolute idealism, building complete systems in which reality is the unfolding of mind or spirit.
questions: Is there anything out there that my mind could never, even in principle, know?
Could one single starting point explain everything, from logic to art to politics?
How can I be free if I am also part of a nature run by causes?

themes.name: From Kant to absolute idealism
themes.text: Kant held that we know only appearances, not things in themselves. Fichte, Schelling and Hegel went further: a thing that could never be an object for consciousness, they argued, is a contradiction in terms.

themes.name: One system for everything
themes.text: The idealists wanted one system covering logic, metaphysics, ethics, politics and art. Fichte, Schelling and Hegel tried to derive it all from a single first principle, called the absolute (the unconditioned starting point).

themes.name: Becoming a self through others
themes.text: Fichte argued that you become a self only when another free person calls on you to respect their freedom. Hegel built on this: self-consciousness depends on mutual recognition, and patterns of recognition make up social life.

themes.name: Nature and art
themes.text: Schelling treated nature as a living, productive whole that includes us, not just matter obeying laws. He held that art can reveal what philosophy cannot turn into an object of knowledge, a view Hegel later disputed.

themes.name: Spirit learning through history
themes.text: Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit follows a series of ways of seeing the world, each breaking down on its own contradictions and giving rise to the next. Its story maps onto Western history from the Greeks to his own day.

reactedAgainst.text: The limits Kant had placed on knowledge, especially his unknowable things in themselves, and the old split between rationalism and empiricism.

schools.name: Utilitarianism
schools.description: The moral theory that right actions are those that produce the greatest happiness.
questions: Is an action right or wrong simply because of what it leads to?
Does my own happiness count for more than a stranger's?
What good does this law or custom actually do?

themes.name: Consequences decide
themes.text: Utilitarianism is a kind of consequentialism: whether an act or policy is right depends entirely on its results. Bentham even valued liberty only for what it brings about, not for its own sake.

themes.name: Pleasure and pain
themes.text: For the classical utilitarians, the good to be produced is pleasure and the bad is pain. Bentham called pleasure and pain our two 'sovereign masters', ruling all we do, say and think.

themes.name: Everyone counts the same
themes.text: Utilitarianism is impartial: one person's happiness counts no more than anyone else's. Sidgwick put it as the good of any one person mattering no more, from the point of view of the universe, than anyone else's.

themes.name: A tool for reform
themes.text: Godwin, Bentham and Mill wanted to change useless and corrupt laws and social practices, so they needed a moral theory to use as a critical tool. Their driving question was 'What good is it?'

themes.name: Higher and lower pleasures
themes.text: Mill broke with Bentham by arguing that pleasures differ in quality as well as amount. The better pleasure is the one preferred by people who have experienced both.

reactedAgainst.text: Laws and customs defended by tradition, legal 'fictions' or mere disgust rather than by their real effects on people's happiness.

schools.name: Marxism
schools.description: Marx's materialist theory of history and critique of capitalism: alienation, class struggle, ideology and the case for communism.
schools.debatable: Also a political movement; here only the philosophical tradition.
questions: Why does my work so often feel as if it isn't really mine?
Do ideas drive history, or do economics and material life drive our ideas?
Why do unequal societies stay so stable, and could things be organized differently?

themes.name: Alienation
themes.text: Alienation means being cut off from something that properly belongs to you. Marx argued that workers under capitalism are separated from what they make, from their own activity, from each other and from their human nature.

themes.name: Historical materialism
themes.text: Societies rise and fall as they first help and then hold back human productive power. A society's economic structure shapes its politics, law and ideas, rather than the other way round.

themes.name: Class and exploitation
themes.text: History moves through a series of economic systems marked by class struggle. Marx traced capitalist profit to surplus value taken from workers, though whether this depends on his labor theory of value is debated.

sources.section: 5.1 Production and class, base and superstructure

themes.name: Ideology and false appearances
themes.text: Some widely shared beliefs may hide how society really works, helping class-divided societies stay stable. Lukács later argued that capitalism makes social relations look like relations between things.

themes.name: People remake their world
themes.text: Marx combined materialism with the idealists' stress on human activity: people transform their world through material work, not just thought. Lukács framed Marxism as a self-conscious transformation of society.

reactedAgainst.text: German idealism, which Marx and Engels said mistook ideas for real things, and the capitalist society of their day.

schools.name: Existentialism
schools.dateRange: roots in the 1840s (Kierkegaard); movement in mid-20th-century France
schools.description: Philosophy that starts from concrete, first-person human existence: freedom, anxiety, authenticity and the search for meaning. It includes Camus's philosophy of the absurd, though Camus rejected the existentialist label.
schools.debatable: Absurdism is folded in: SEP files Camus's 'absurdity' among existentialist themes (§5.1), but Camus denied being an existentialist (SEP Camus, §1). Kierkegaard and Nietzsche are forerunners, not members.
questions: If nothing hands me a purpose, how do I live?
Am I living my own life, or just doing what everyone else does?
What do I do with the anxiety of being free to choose?

questionSources.section: 1. Nihilism and the Crisis of Modernity
1. The Paradoxes of Camus’s Absurdist Philosophy

themes.name: Existence before essence
themes.text: No fixed human nature decides who we are; we turn up first and define ourselves through our choices. Sartre gave this its famous slogan, yet we still face given facts such as our body and our history.

themes.name: Freedom and anxiety
themes.text: Anxiety shows me that I alone must answer for whatever I choose among my possibilities. Kierkegaard called it the dizziness of freedom, and the existentialists ask us to face it rather than flee.

sources.section: 2. Kierkegaard’s Analysis of Human Existence: Despair, Social Critique, and Anxiety

themes.name: Authenticity versus the crowd
themes.text: We tend to drift along with Kierkegaard's 'public' or Nietzsche's 'herd', living by borrowed norms. Sartre and Beauvoir call this kind of self-deception 'bad faith': denying either our freedom or the facts of our situation.

sources.section: 1. Nihilism and the Crisis of Modernity

themes.name: Meaning without guarantees
themes.text: Nietzsche diagnosed nihilism, the loss of any overarching purpose once belief in God collapsed. Camus called the clash between our hunger for meaning and a silent universe 'the absurd', though he denied being an existentialist.

sources.section: 1. Nihilism and the Crisis of Modernity
1. The Paradoxes of Camus’s Absurdist Philosophy

themes.name: My freedom needs yours
themes.text: Existentialist ethics starts from the idea that no moral order is given in advance. But Beauvoir and Sartre argued that willing my own freedom commits me to willing the freedom of others.

sources.section: 5. The Ethics of Ambiguity: Bad Faith, the Appeal, the Artist

reactedAgainst.text: Philosophy's detached 'view from nowhere' and all-explaining systems like Hegel's, and the loss of meaning in a secular, mass, bureaucratic modern world.

sources.section: 1. Nihilism and the Crisis of Modernity
1. The Paradoxes of Camus’s Absurdist Philosophy

schools.name: Pragmatism
schools.description: An American philosophy that clarifies ideas by their practical consequences and treats inquiry and truth in terms of action.
questions: What difference would it actually make if this idea were true?
Can I hold beliefs without being certain and still make progress?
If knowledge grows from solving real problems, how should we learn and live together?

themes.name: Meaning lies in practical effects
themes.text: Peirce's pragmatic maxim says that the meaning of an idea is the practical effects we would expect if it were true. James used the same test to dissolve disputes: if neither side would make any practical difference, the quarrel is idle.

themes.name: Truth tied to inquiry and use
themes.text: Peirce saw truth as the opinion that inquirers would ultimately agree on. James called true whatever proves good to believe, and Rorty later said there is little of substance to say about truth at all.

themes.name: Fallible, not skeptical
themes.text: Pragmatists rejected Descartes' method of doubting everything at once. We can be wrong, but further inquiry can find and correct our errors, so we should be fallibilists (people who accept they may be wrong) rather than skeptics.

themes.name: Inquiry as problem-solving
themes.text: Peirce described inquiry as the struggle to replace doubt with settled belief. Dewey saw it as turning an unsettled, problematic situation into a settled one.

themes.name: Philosophy for social life
themes.text: A second generation, shaped above all by Dewey, turned pragmatism toward politics, education and social improvement. For Dewey, democracy was a whole way of living together, and schools were places to practise it.

reactedAgainst.text: Descartes-style philosophy that seeks certainty by doubting everything, and the picture of knowledge as a mind mirroring an outside world.

schools.name: Phenomenology
schools.description: The careful description of experience as it is lived from the first-person point of view, founded by Husserl.
schools.debatable: Both a method and a movement; it overlaps heavily with existentialism (Heidegger, Sartre and Merleau-Ponty are in both).
questions: What is it actually like to see, remember or feel something, described from the inside?
If I set aside whether the world really exists and just look at how things show up for me, what do I find?
How does having a body shape the way I perceive and act in the world?

questionSources.section: 4. The History and Varieties of Phenomenology
4. The History and Varieties of Phenomenology

themes.name: Experience is always 'of' something
themes.text: Phenomenologists call this intentionality: every experience points at something, like a tree I see or a meal I want. They study how an experience presents its object, through the meaning it has for me, not just whether the object is there.

sources.section: 4. The History and Varieties of Phenomenology

themes.name: Bracketing the world
themes.text: Husserl proposed the epoché (a Greek word for holding back belief): you set aside the everyday assumption that the world exists apart from you. That frees you to describe how things are actually given in experience, instead of how you think they must be.

sources.section: 4. The History and Varieties of Phenomenology

themes.name: Being-in-the-world
themes.text: Heidegger argued you can't bracket the world, because we are always already in it. Our most basic way of relating to things is practical, like using a hammer, inside a web of tools and other people.

sources.section: 4. The History and Varieties of Phenomenology

themes.name: The lived body
themes.text: Merleau-Ponty put the body at the centre of experience. Your body is neither just a machine nor just an idea in the mind; it is you, engaged with the things and people you perceive.

sources.section: 4. The History and Varieties of Phenomenology

themes.name: The lifeworld comes first
themes.text: The lifeworld is the everyday world we live and feel at home in, full of cups to drink from and chairs to sit on. Husserl held that science grows out of this world and should not dismiss it as mere illusion.

reactedAgainst.text: It pushed back against psychologism (the view that logic can be reduced to psychology) and against reductionism and scientism, which treat the measurable world of science as the only real one.

sources.section: 4. The History and Varieties of Phenomenology
3. The transcendental turn: Epoché, phenomenological reduction, and transcendental idealism

schools.name: Analytic Philosophy
schools.description: Philosophy pursued through logical and linguistic analysis and clear argument, dominant in British and American universities; its logical positivist phase held that only verifiable statements are meaningful.
schools.debatable: A broad tradition with several phases (IEP counts five); Logical Positivism (Vienna Circle, 1924–1936) is folded in as its third phase, as IEP treats it (decision L17). Whether Frege counts as a founder is contested (IEP §2c).
questions: What exactly do my words mean, and can getting clear about that make old philosophical puzzles disappear?
If no observation could ever check a statement, does it mean anything at all?
Does a word get its meaning from the thing it names, or from how people use it?

questionSources.section: d. Logical Atomism and Wittgenstein’s Tractatus
a. Logical Positivism and the Vienna Circle

themes.name: Analysis: getting meanings clear
themes.text: Moore and Russell turned away from grand philosophical systems toward narrow problems tackled with precision. They worked by analysing the meanings of words and sentences, which is where the name 'analytic' comes from.

sources.section: 1. The Revolution of Moore and Russell: Cambridge Realism and The Linguistic Turn

themes.name: Logic as a new tool
themes.text: Frege built a new formal logic, and Russell refined it. Russell hoped it could reveal the hidden 'logical form' of everyday sentences and clear up confusions that ordinary grammar creates.

themes.name: Language as a picture of the world
themes.text: Logical atomism held that the world is made of simple facts, and that a properly built sentence mirrors their structure. Wittgenstein's Tractatus concluded that much traditional philosophy tries to say what cannot be said.

sources.section: d. Logical Atomism and Wittgenstein’s Tractatus

themes.name: Logical positivism (Vienna Circle)
themes.text: In this phase (the Vienna Circle met 1924–1936), a statement counted as meaningful only if experience could check it, unless it was a tautology (true by its logical form alone). Metaphysics was ruled out as meaningless; critics noted the principle seems to fail its own test.

sources.section: a. Logical Positivism and the Vienna Circle

themes.name: Meaning as use
themes.text: The later Wittgenstein dropped the picture idea: a word's meaning lies in its use within a shared 'language game' and way of life. Philosophy then becomes a kind of therapy that untangles misuses of language.

reactedAgainst.text: It began as a break with British Idealism, the view then dominant in British universities that the world is really one spiritual whole, and then with grand system-building philosophy in general.

schools.name: Critical Theory (Frankfurt School)
schools.description: Western Marxist social philosophy that joins philosophy with social science to criticise domination and aim at emancipation.
schools.debatable: SEP notes a narrow sense (the Frankfurt School, used here) and broader senses of 'critical theory'.
questions: Why do people accept social conditions that work against their own interests?
Can the same reason that freed us from fear turn into a tool of control?
What would a theory look like that doesn't just describe society but helps change it?

questionSources.section: 5. One-Dimensional Thinking and the Democratic Rejection of Democracy

themes.name: Theory that aims to free people
themes.text: Horkheimer contrasted critical theory with 'traditional' theory, which takes the existing social order as given. Critical theory joins philosophy with social science to expose domination and support change.

themes.name: Why people accept domination
themes.text: Borrowing from Marx, they studied ideology: beliefs that make exploitation feel natural or even fair. Marcuse described a 'comfortable' unfreedom in which people no longer think critically or demand change.

sources.section: 5. One-Dimensional Thinking and the Democratic Rejection of Democracy

themes.name: Enlightenment turned against itself
themes.text: Horkheimer and Adorno argued that reason, meant to free us from fear, narrowed into instrumental reason (working out means without asking about ends). Pushed far enough, it becomes a new kind of domination.

themes.name: The culture industry
themes.text: Mass culture, they argued, is not made by the masses but manufactured like any other product. Standardised entertainment turns culture into a commodity and helps keep things as they are.

themes.name: Reason in conversation
themes.text: Habermas, of the second generation, looked for reason in everyday communication. His public sphere is a space where equals debate shared concerns and are moved by the better argument.

reactedAgainst.text: It reacted against 'traditional', positivist theory that treats the social order as a given fact, and it revised Marxism, since the workers Marx expected to bring change had turned toward fascism instead.

sources.section: 1. Critical Theory: Historical and Philosophical Background

schools.name: Post-structuralism
schools.description: French thought that grew out of structuralism to question stable meaning, the self-present subject and claims to foundations, through deconstruction and genealogy.
schools.debatable: SEP has no entry by this name; it is covered under 'Postmodernism' (which says these thinkers are often called poststructuralists) and the Derrida and Foucault entries. The two labels overlap.
questions: Am I really the author of my own thoughts, or am I shaped by structures I never chose?
Do the categories we treat as natural, like 'normal' or 'mad', have a history?
Do the big pairs we think in, like essence and appearance or speech and writing, quietly rank one side above the other?

themes.name: Decentring the subject
themes.text: The self is not the fixed starting point of truth and knowledge. It is shaped in advance by history, language and social practices, in ways we are never fully aware of.

themes.name: Genealogy: no pure origins
themes.text: Following Nietzsche, Foucault traced how ideas and institutions arose from accidents and conflicts rather than from one clean origin. Showing this history loosens the hold of what seems natural.

themes.name: Power and knowledge
themes.text: Foucault argued that modern knowledge and control are tied together. Exams, for instance, both find out the truth about people and shape how they behave.

themes.name: Deconstruction
themes.text: Derrida read texts to expose ranked oppositions, such as voice over writing, and to unsettle them. He held that meaning is never fully present but arises from differences between signs.

themes.name: Difference that creates
themes.text: Deleuze treated difference as productive in itself, not merely as the opposite or negation of identity. He criticised thinking that reduces everything to sameness, opposition and resemblance.

reactedAgainst.text: It grew out of structuralism but turned against the idea of a self-present subject as the origin of meaning, as in Sartre's starting point, and against claims to firm foundations and stable meaning.

sources.section: 3. Basic Argumentation and its Implications: Time, Hearing-Oneself-Speak, the Secret, and Sovereignty

schools.name: Feminist Philosophy
schools.dateRange: 1970s – present as an academic field (forerunners: Wollstonecraft 1792, Beauvoir 1949)
schools.description: Philosophy that criticises institutions and theories that have favoured men and rethinks sex, gender, knowledge and ethics.
schools.debatable: Not a single school but a field that works within every tradition (analytic, continental, pragmatist; SEP §3).
questions: Why have so many institutions and ideas favoured men, and what would a just society look like?
Is being a woman something you are born as, or something you become?
What changes when philosophy takes care, dependency and women's lives seriously?

questionSources.section: 7. The Second Sex: Woman As Other

themes.name: Ending gender-based oppression
themes.text: Feminism is both a way of thinking and a political movement aimed at ending oppression based on gender. It asks how norms have excluded people and how a just society would look.

themes.name: The 'neutral' view was male
themes.text: Philosophy often claimed to speak from a neutral, universal point of view. Feminists showed that these supposedly neutral approaches were in fact shaped around men.

themes.name: Starting from embodied lives
themes.text: Feminist philosophers start by seeing people as embodied, and their work tends to be contextual and rooted in lived experience. Beauvoir's study of women's lived bodies is a founding example.

sources.section: 7. The Second Sex: Woman As Other

themes.name: Woman as the Other
themes.text: Beauvoir argued that men have been treated as the essential being and women as the Other. Myths of femininity trap women in that role, which is why she says one becomes a woman.

sources.section: 7. The Second Sex: Woman As Other

themes.name: Education, independence, equal rights
themes.text: Early feminists argued that women need education, reason and the means to support themselves. Wollstonecraft called for women's rights and representation; Taylor Mill's essay demanded equality in all rights.

reactedAgainst.text: It challenged institutions and theories that have historically favoured men, and philosophy's claim to speak from a neutral, universal point of view.
